claims.text: An intact passive oxide film protects a high-entropy alloy from corrosion.
Mechanical wear continuously removes or damages the passive film.
Damage to the passive film exposes fresh, unpassivated alloy substrate.
Freshly exposed alloy substrate is more reactive and rapidly corrodes in a corrosive environment.
The coupled tribocorrosion response is governed by wear-induced passive-film removal followed by accelerated localized corrosion.
A Cantor-type high-entropy alloy can have a stable native or engineered passive oxide layer before degradation.
Under minimal wear, the passive film remains largely intact.
Chloride-containing electrolytes can attack exposed metal and deteriorate passive films.
Cyclic passive-film removal combined with insufficient film reformation produces wear-corrosion synergy and accelerates corrosion.
Corrosion degradation compromises surface mechanical integrity and can consequently increase wear.
Relative to a minimal-wear baseline, controlled wear will increase total degradation chiefly through enhanced localized corrosion.
Wear-track depth or area may increase because corrosion has compromised the surface.
The proposed wear-corrosion enhancement should be minimized or absent in inert environments or where passive films rapidly self-heal.
The magnitude of degradation acceleration depends on the balance between passive-film removal and passive-film reformation rates.
Failure of verified passive-film removal to produce a statistically significant increase in corrosion metrics or total degradation would falsify the proposed mechanism.
